title: Calvin–Benson–Bassham cycle, with sucrose and starch

images.caption: Van Helmont's willow (Latin original): 5 lb grew to 169 lb in five years; the soil lost ≈2 oz
images.credit: van Helmont JB 1648, Ortus medicinae (Amsterdam: L. Elzevir), p. 109; Wellcome Collection copy via Internet Archive (b33276079, scan leaf 0155), Public Domain Mark
images.note: Where does plant mass come from? He answered 'water'; the carbon from the air is the cycle's job. The passage starts at the foot of p. 108.

images.caption: Tobacco chloroplast in TEM: granular stroma (S) around grana (GT) and stroma thylakoids (ST), inside the envelope (EM)
images.credit: Staehelin & Paolillo 2020, Photosynth Res 145:237, Fig. 3 (micrograph from Staehelin 1986); CC BY 4.0
images.note: The compartment where the cycle runs. Unaltered figure with the authors' labels; scale bar 0.5 µm per the caption. The deck's chloroplast-tem.jpg is a relabelled crop of it.

images.caption: The 11 cycle enzymes per 3 CO₂; thioredoxin-activated enzymes in blue, RuBisCO activase green, CP12 red
images.credit: Michelet et al. 2013, Front Plant Sci 4:470, Fig. 1; CC BY
images.note: The one image for light activation: shows which steps light switches on (PRK, GAPDH, FBPase, SBPase) on the whole cycle.

images.caption: Cycle counted per 3 CO₂: 3 RuBP → 6 PGA → 6 GAP; one GAP leaves, five rebuild 3 Ru5P
images.credit: Sharkey 2019, Photosynth Res 140:235, Fig. 3; © Springer Nature
images.note: Carbon counts and costs in one picture (3 + 6 ATP, 6 NADPH per 3 CO₂): the template for the C3 cycle redraw.

images.caption: (a) Calvin with Jacques Mayaudon and Andrew Benson, 1950s; (b) Bassham, Benson and Alex Wilson at the Radiation Laboratory
images.credit: Govindjee, Nonomura & Lichtenthaler 2019, Photosynth Res 143:1, Fig. 2 (archives of A. Nonomura); © Springer Nature
images.note: All three names of the cycle in period photos. Panel b names are printed under the photo; panel a order is not printed.

images.caption: Melvin Calvin in 1961, the year he alone received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry
images.credit: Donald Cooksey / Berkeley Lab, 26 Oct 1961 (LBNL Biosciences, 'Calvin cycle continued'); © The Regents of the University of California
images.note: Same photo as Govindjee et al. 2019 Fig. 8b (tie with porphyrin motifs made by his mother).

images.caption: Andrew Benson tending the culture system that grew the algae for the lollipop experiments
images.credit: Courtesy Dee Benson; Nonomura et al. 2017, Photosynth Res 134:93, Fig. 2 (caption as given by LBNL Biosciences)
images.note: Only 388 px wide. Alternative: 'Dr Andrew Benson 2007', Jess Gordon, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 (668 px).

images.caption: James A. Bassham, later director of chemical biodynamics at the Lawrence Radiation Laboratory
images.credit: Steve Gerber / Berkeley Lab, archive no. XBD9705-02084 (LBNL Biosciences); © The Regents of the University of California
images.note: The only clear solo portrait of Bassham found online (528 px); photo date not given.

images.caption: The 'lollipop': a flat glass flask of algae lit from both sides, given ¹⁴CO₂, drained into alcohol below
images.credit: Robert M. Couto / Berkeley Lab, colorized (LBNL Biosciences); © The Regents of the University of California
images.note: Colorized by LBNL. Same apparatus as Calvin's Nobel lecture Fig. 3, which is only a coarse 1-bit scan.

images.caption: Autoradiogram of a Chlorella extract after 5 s in ¹⁴CO₂: label mainly in PGA and sugar phosphates
images.credit: Calvin 1961, Nobel lecture 'The path of carbon in photosynthesis', Fig. 6; © The Nobel Foundation 1961
images.note: Short pulse: the first stable product is 3-PGA. Pair with k.

images.caption: Same after 30 s: label has spread to sucrose, UDPG, amino acids (alanine, serine, glycine) and organic acids
images.credit: Calvin 1961, Nobel lecture 'The path of carbon in photosynthesis', Fig. 5; © The Nobel Foundation 1961
images.note: Long pulse, same solvents and orientation as j, so the two can sit side by side.

images.caption: The first drawing of the cycle (1954), with 'RuBP' and enzyme names added later by Sharkey
images.credit: Bassham, Benson, Kay, Harris, Wilson & Calvin 1954, J Am Chem Soc 76:1760, Fig. 7; reproduced and annotated in Sharkey 2019, Photosynth Res 140:235, Fig. 2
images.note: How the discoverers drew it: C5 → C6 (β-keto acid) → 2 C3, with the light-driven [H] and ATP feeding in.

images.caption: Light off: PGA jumps and RuBP falls to zero within a minute; regenerating RuBP needs light
images.credit: Calvin 1961, Nobel lecture, Fig. 15 (Bassham's data, Chlorella); © The Nobel Foundation 1961
images.note: The classic evidence that the cycle closes through light-dependent reduction and RuBP regeneration.

images.caption: RuBisCO: plant L₈S₈ (spinach, PDB 1RCX; small subunits blue/purple) beside the bacterial L₂ dimer (PDB 9RUB)
images.credit: Goodsell DS 2000, PDB-101 Molecule of the Month 11 'RuBisCO', doi:10.2210/rcsb_pdb/mom_2000_11; CC BY 4.0
images.note: Space-filling atomic models; the board's only structure image (Andersson & Backlund 2008 figure is on the wanted list).

images.caption: Global RuBisCO: ≈7×10¹⁴ g on land fixes ≈1.2×10¹⁷ g C per year, ≈0.03 reactions per site per second
images.credit: Bar-On & Milo 2019, PNAS 116:4738, Fig. 3; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
images.note: RuBisCO's bulk and slowness in one line. The paper says it is not clear that RuBisCO is the most abundant protein.

images.caption: Triose phosphate leaves through the translocator to make sucrose in the cytosol; starch is made inside the chloroplast
images.credit: Sharkey 2024, Plant Physiol 195:67, Fig. 1; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
images.note: Canonical day-time carbon export (triose phosphate utilization); redraw, do not modify (ND licence).

images.caption: Leaf plastids in TEM: starch at end of day (B–E), mostly gone by end of night except guard cells (F–I)
images.credit: Streb & Zeeman 2012, The Arabidopsis Book 10:e0160, Fig. 4; © American Society of Plant Biologists
images.note: Arabidopsis. Rows: epidermis, mesophyll, bundle sheath, guard cell; A is a toluidine-blue leaf section (its guard-cell inset renders blank in the PMC file). Zeeman lab, ETH Zurich.

images.caption: Iodine-stained rosettes: wild type, starch-poor pgm1, isa1, and starch-excess sex1, beside their diel starch curves
images.credit: Streb & Zeeman 2012, The Arabidopsis Book 10:e0160, Fig. 1; © American Society of Plant Biologists
images.note: The iodine screen that found the starch mutants. Low resolution (483 px); a sharper copy is on the wanted list.

images.caption: Arabidopsis leaf starch: after an unexpected dusk at 8 h, breakdown slows so starch still lasts to dawn
images.credit: Graf, Schlereth, Stitt & Smith 2010, PNAS 107:9458, Fig. 1; © National Academy of Sciences
images.note: Panel A is the key: squares 12 h day, diamonds early night. Panel B (starvation genes) can be cropped off.

images.caption: Morning glory phloem: SEM of sieve plates at 1, 4 and 7 m along the stem, with sieve-tube dimensions
images.credit: Knoblauch et al. 2016, eLife 5:e15341, Fig. 1; CC BY 4.0
images.note: The pipe that carries sucrose out of the leaf. Same paper, Fig. 2—figure supplement 1A, shows sieve elements with companion cells.
